cards.statement: Memorystore for Redis Standard Tier can keep a read-endpoint connection on one replica for its lifetime.
cards.explanation: The read endpoint balances connections across replicas. Reusing one connection keeps its read queries on the same replica, which matters when distributing a cache's read load.

cards.statement: Cloud Run services handle bidirectional gRPC streams over HTTP/2.
cards.explanation: A Cloud Run service handles streaming gRPC interfaces when the service uses HTTP/2. Bidirectional streaming is a supported gRPC interaction.

cards.statement: By default, Workflows connectors end a long-running call when the API accepts the operation.
cards.explanation: Workflows connectors wait for a long-running operation to succeed or fail. The API's initial acceptance response does not complete the connector call.
cards.misconception: A connector treats acceptance of an asynchronous operation as its completion.

cards.statement: Cloud Tasks uses its dispatch rate as the ceiling on simultaneous handler executions.
cards.explanation: Cloud Tasks separates dispatches per second from concurrent dispatches. Configure the concurrency limit to bound the tasks running at once.
cards.misconception: The rate setting and the concurrency setting limit the same quantity.

source.title: Configure queue routing, limits, and retries

cards.statement: Eventarc Standard can guarantee source order when delivering related application events.
cards.explanation: Eventarc Standard provides no delivery-order guarantee. An application that depends on sequence needs to handle events that arrive out of order.
cards.misconception: Event delivery preserves the order in which the source emits related events.

cards.statement: Cloud Run keeps configured traffic percentages for returning clients when session affinity is enabled.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run's best-effort session affinity takes precedence over traffic splits. Returning clients can skew the observed proportions across revisions.
cards.misconception: Session affinity preserves configured traffic proportions for returning clients.

cards.statement: Cloud Run's CPU autoscaler uses the busiest vCPU in a multi-vCPU instance.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run averages CPU utilization across an instance's vCPUs. A busy single thread can leave that average low when other vCPUs are idle.
cards.misconception: A CPU hotspot determines Cloud Run's CPU utilization signal.

source.title: About instance autoscaling in Cloud Run services

cards.statement: Cloud Run leaves isolation between concurrent requests in one service instance to the application code.
cards.explanation: With concurrency above 1, Cloud Run provides no isolation between requests one instance processes at once. Shared mutable state, such as globals in a threaded server, needs concurrency-safe code.

cards.statement: Cloud Tasks marks an HTTP task complete when its handler returns a 2xx response.
cards.explanation: Cloud Tasks removes an HTTP task after the handler acknowledges it with a 2xx response. The handler's response is the queue's completion signal.

cards.statement: Attaching a user-managed service identity to a Cloud Run service requires the deployer to hold actAs on that account.
cards.explanation: The deployer needs iam.serviceAccounts.actAs on the service account, for example through the Service Account User role, to attach it to a Cloud Run service or revision.

cards.statement: Cloud Run grants storage permissions when a user-managed service account becomes a service identity.
cards.explanation: Attaching a user-managed service account selects an identity. A developer grants that account the needed Cloud Storage IAM permissions separately.
cards.misconception: Attaching a runtime identity automatically authorizes access to application resources.

cards.statement: ADC checks an environment-specified credential file before its local credential file.
cards.explanation: Application Default Credentials checks the environment-specified file first, then the local ADC file, then the attached service account.

cards.statement: ADC requires a private key in a credential file supplied through GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS.
cards.explanation: The ADC credential file can be a Workload Identity Federation configuration. Such a configuration describes external credentials instead of holding a service account private key.
cards.misconception: An ADC credential file is necessarily a service account key file.

cards.statement: Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets IAM grant resource access to a Kubernetes service account principal.
cards.explanation: IAM can authorize a principal representing a workload's Kubernetes service account. That Kubernetes identity remains distinct from an IAM service account.

source.title: About Workload Identity Federation for GKE

cards.statement: Cloud Run can refresh a secret environment variable in a running instance when a new secret version appears.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run resolves secret environment variables when an instance starts. Publishing a newer version does not replace the value inside a running instance.
cards.misconception: Secret environment variables track newly published secret versions during an instance's lifetime.

cards.statement: IAM-authenticated Cloud Run service calls require a Google-signed ID token from the caller.
cards.explanation: For IAM-authenticated service-to-service calls, the caller sends a Google-signed ID token. Its audience identifies the receiving service or a configured custom audience.

cards.statement: Artifact Analysis updates vulnerability metadata for recently pulled, scanned container images.
cards.explanation: Continuous analysis uses new vulnerability information to update metadata for scanned images whose recent pulls keep analysis active.

cards.statement: Secret Manager creates a new secret version when a rotation schedule becomes due.
cards.explanation: Secret Manager sends a rotation notification to the configured Pub/Sub topics. Application rotation code acts on that message to create the new version.
cards.misconception: A Secret Manager rotation schedule performs the application's secret replacement.

source.title: Create rotation schedules in Secret Manager

cards.statement: Firestore Standard edition automatically builds a missing composite index when an app submits a query.
cards.explanation: A developer creates composite indexes for queries that need them. Firestore Standard edition reports a missing index instead of building it on demand.
cards.misconception: Automatic basic indexing also creates composite indexes on demand.

cards.statement: A Firestore query ordered by a field omits documents that lack that field, even when they match its filters.
cards.explanation: In Firestore, an orderBy clause also filters on the field's existence, so documents without the field drop out of results silently. Give every document the field or run a separate query.

cards.statement: Firestore server client libraries automatically delete subcollection documents when deleting a parent.
cards.explanation: A Firestore server client's document deletion leaves subcollection documents in place. Applications need a separate recursive cleanup when those descendants should also be removed.
cards.misconception: Deleting a parent document through a server client cascades to its subcollections.

cards.statement: Spanner interleaved child tables put the parent's primary key at the start of the child's primary key.
cards.explanation: A Spanner interleaved child's primary key begins with the parent's key columns in the same order. This key structure ties related child rows to their parent in storage.

cards.statement: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL read replicas expose a primary's committed write as soon as the commit returns.
cards.explanation: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL replicas receive and apply the primary's changes separately. A primary commit can succeed while a replica still awaits those changes, so its query results can lag.
cards.misconception: A successful primary commit guarantees immediate visibility through its read replicas.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage object listings include newly created objects after a successful create response.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage object listing is strongly consistent. A list request after a successful object creation reflects the newly created object.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage signed URLs can authorize object requests through JSON API endpoints.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage signed URLs work with XML API endpoints. The caller uses the signed URL with its permitted operation through that interface.
cards.misconception: Cloud Storage signed URLs work interchangeably with its JSON and XML API endpoints.

cards.statement: A Firestore server client creates an empty document when it constructs a document reference.
cards.explanation: Constructing a Firestore document reference creates a local object pointing to a database path. A document appears when application code writes its data.
cards.misconception: Constructing a document reference materializes an empty stored document.

cards.statement: BigQuery Storage Write API gRPC writes encode JSON column values as strings in protocol buffers.
cards.explanation: For the BigQuery Storage Write API's gRPC interface, represent JSON column values as strings in the row protocol buffer. BigQuery then writes those values to the table's JSON column.

source.title: Work with JSON data in GoogleSQL

cards.statement: Cloud Shell preserves source files in its home directory across regular development sessions.
cards.explanation: Cloud Shell's home directory uses persistent storage in its regular mode. Keeping a source checkout there carries it into later sessions.

cards.statement: Cloud Workstations automatically rebuilds a custom image when Google updates its base image.
cards.explanation: The team maintaining a custom Cloud Workstations image rebuilds it to incorporate base-image updates. Google recommends setting up a pipeline to perform that rebuild.
cards.misconception: Google's base-image updates automatically rebuild an organization's derived development image.

cards.statement: Cloud Code for VS Code uses Skaffold to run and debug an existing Kubernetes application.
cards.explanation: Cloud Code uses the application's Skaffold configuration for its Kubernetes development workflow. The IDE integration sets up the run or debug session around that configuration.

source.title: Use an existing application in Cloud Code for VS Code

cards.statement: The Firestore Standard edition emulator rejects a query whose required composite index is missing.
cards.explanation: The Firestore emulator executes valid queries without checking composite indexes. Verify index requirements against a real Firestore Standard edition database before deployment.
cards.misconception: A successful emulator query proves the production database has the composite indexes it needs.
cards.volatilityNote: The emulator's production-feature parity can change as its implementation evolves.

cards.statement: Cloud Workstations' persistent home disk replaces files a custom image added under /home at build time.
cards.explanation: By default a persistent disk attaches over /home when the container starts, overwriting build-time changes there. Install tools outside /home or modify /home at runtime.

cards.statement: The Pub/Sub emulator can validate an application's IAM policy changes during local development.
cards.explanation: The Pub/Sub emulator omits IAM operations. Its local behavior therefore provides no validation of the application's production IAM policy changes.
cards.misconception: The Pub/Sub emulator implements production IAM operations for local permission validation.
cards.volatilityNote: Supported emulator operations can expand as the emulator evolves.

source.title: Testing apps locally with the emulator

cards.statement: Firestore server client libraries automatically use FIRESTORE_EMULATOR_HOST to route calls to a local emulator.
cards.explanation: Set FIRESTORE_EMULATOR_HOST to the emulator's host and port before creating a Firestore server client. The client then sends requests to that emulator endpoint.

cards.statement: The Bigtable emulator restores application data from the previous run when it starts again.
cards.explanation: The Bigtable emulator keeps data in memory, so a later run starts with an empty store. Local development setup needs to recreate the tables and data it uses.
cards.misconception: The Bigtable emulator persists its data across process restarts.

cards.statement: The Node.js Functions Framework detects HTTP or CloudEvent signatures from handler parameters.
cards.explanation: Node.js code declares the signature type by registering its handler with functions.http or functions.cloudEvent. The framework does not read the handler's parameter list to decide.
cards.misconception: The Node.js Functions Framework infers the trigger signature from the handler's parameters.

cards.statement: Cloud Build lets a later step inherit shell-exported variables from the preceding build step.
cards.explanation: Cloud Build runs steps in separate containers. A shell export stays in its step's process environment instead of becoming the next step's environment.
cards.misconception: A shell environment survives the transition between Cloud Build steps.

cards.statement: Cloud Build lets independent steps execute concurrently through explicit waitFor dependencies.
cards.explanation: Cloud Build schedules steps according to their declared dependencies. Independent branches can overlap instead of following the build file's sequential order.

source.title: Configuring the order of build steps

cards.statement: A Cloud Build step's name field specifies the registry destination of its build output.
cards.explanation: The name field identifies the container image Cloud Build runs for that step. It selects the step's execution tools rather than naming the step's output artifact.
cards.misconception: A build step's container image field describes its output artifact.

cards.statement: Cloud Build supplies $SHORT_SHA as a default substitution to builds that a trigger invokes.
cards.explanation: Trigger-invoked builds get default substitutions such as $COMMIT_SHA and $SHORT_SHA. A build started with gcloud builds submit gets these values only when the developer passes them.

cards.statement: Cloud Build triggers require an explicit dynamic-substitution setting to expand nested build substitutions.
cards.explanation: Cloud Build enables dynamic substitutions for trigger-invoked builds. A trigger resolves references within substitution values regardless of that setting in the build file.
cards.misconception: A trigger needs the same explicit dynamic-substitution setting as a manually invoked build.

cards.statement: Cloud Build pushes Artifact Registry images declared in its images field after build steps succeed.
cards.explanation: Cloud Build's images field declares output images for the final push phase. Names pointing to Artifact Registry send those images to the specified repositories.

cards.statement: Cloud Build's global environment setting can take precedence over a matching step-level env value.
cards.explanation: Cloud Build uses the step-level environment value when a variable appears at both levels. A build step therefore overrides the build's global value for that variable.
cards.misconception: Global build environment values outrank a step's matching values.

cards.statement: Cloud Build generates native provenance for an Artifact Registry image uploaded by a docker push step alone.
cards.explanation: Cloud Build's native container provenance uses the images output field. An explicit docker push used as the upload mechanism does not generate that provenance.
cards.misconception: An explicit image push produces the same native provenance as Cloud Build's image output mechanism.

cards.statement: Cloud Build requires generated provenance for build success when requestedVerifyOption is VERIFIED.
cards.explanation: The VERIFIED setting makes Cloud Build check that provenance metadata is generated. Failure to generate the requested evidence prevents a successful build result.

cards.statement: A local CloudEvent test reaches Functions Framework through an HTTP POST with event metadata and data.
cards.explanation: Send a sample CloudEvent as an HTTP POST to the running Functions Framework's local endpoint. Event metadata in headers and the request body reproduce the documented event invocation.

cards.statement: Functions Framework base64-decodes a Pub/Sub event's message data before a local CloudEvent handler receives it.
cards.explanation: Pub/Sub events carry base64-encoded data values, and the function is expected to decode them. A local sample event therefore needs base64-encoded data as well.
cards.misconception: Functions Framework hands a local handler already-decoded Pub/Sub message data.

cards.statement: Cloud Build attaches every build step's container to a shared local Docker network named cloudbuild.
cards.explanation: Because steps share that network, they can communicate: an integration-test step can call a service container that an earlier step started on the cloudbuild network.

cards.statement: Cloud Build's allowExitCodes takes precedence over allowFailure in a test step that sets both.
cards.explanation: With allowFailure true and allowExitCodes [1], a test step that exits with 2 still fails the build, because only the listed exit codes are tolerated.

cards.statement: Cloud Build executes a teardown step whose waitFor names a failed test step under default failure handling.
cards.explanation: A Cloud Build teardown step that waits on a test step starts after that dependency succeeds under default failure handling. A failed dependency prevents this cleanup step from starting.
cards.misconception: A teardown step's dependency means it runs after test completion regardless of success.

source.title: Configuring the order of build steps

cards.statement: A successful Cloud Build run uploads selected test report files through its artifacts configuration.
cards.explanation: Configure artifacts.objects with the Cloud Storage destination and generated test-report paths. Cloud Build uploads those reports when the build completes successfully.

cards.statement: A Cloud Build integration-test build config can override the service account chosen in its trigger.
cards.explanation: For a triggered Cloud Build integration-test run, the trigger's configured service account controls build identity. Cloud Build ignores the serviceAccount value in the build config for that run.
cards.misconception: The checked-in build configuration's service account takes precedence over its trigger's identity.

cards.statement: Cloud Build private pools reach private VPC resources through a peering connection with the customer's network.
cards.explanation: Private pools run in a Google-owned service producer network that you peer with your VPC, so integration tests can reach private test databases. The default pool cannot peer into a VPC.

cards.statement: Cloud Build starts a test step's timeout while the step waits for its setup dependencies to finish.
cards.explanation: A Cloud Build step's timeout limits its execution time. Waiting for setup dependencies precedes execution and falls outside this per-step limit.
cards.misconception: A step's timeout starts counting while it waits for prerequisite steps.

cards.statement: Cloud Run source deployment with a build uses the Dockerfile supplied in the source directory.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run's source-with-build workflow gives a supplied Dockerfile precedence. Google Cloud's buildpacks build the image when the source directory lacks a Dockerfile.

cards.statement: A Cloud Run service routes incoming requests to an ingress container listening on 127.0.0.1.
cards.explanation: Configure the ingress container to listen on 0.0.0.0 at Cloud Run's configured port. Binding to loopback leaves the service unreachable to Cloud Run.
cards.misconception: Binding the ingress server to loopback suffices for Cloud Run to reach it.

cards.statement: Cloud Run job code picks each task's share of the input from CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX.
cards.explanation: Each task reads its index from CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX and the task total from CLOUD_RUN_TASK_COUNT. Cloud Run runs the tasks; splitting the input among them is the code's job.

cards.statement: API Gateway lets developers replace the OpenAPI definition inside an existing API config.
cards.explanation: API Gateway keeps an API config's uploaded API definition fixed. Publish the changed OpenAPI definition as a new config.
cards.misconception: An existing API config accepts a replacement API definition.

cards.statement: Cloud Run services configured for end-to-end HTTP/2 receive cleartext h2c requests in their ingress container.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run terminates TLS before forwarding a request to the ingress container. Configure the container's HTTP/2 server for cleartext h2c rather than TLS termination.

cards.statement: Cloud Run automatically creates a revision when a developer edits a service's environment variables.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run stores service configuration in immutable revisions. Changing environment variables versions the runtime configuration even when the container image stays the same.

cards.statement: Eventarc derives a Cloud Run event receiver's destination URL path from the trigger's event type.
cards.explanation: The developer configures the Cloud Run destination path in the Eventarc trigger. Eventarc sends events to the root path when the developer leaves this setting unspecified.
cards.misconception: An Eventarc event type determines the receiver's application URL path.

cards.statement: Cloud Functions v2 API supports updating functions created through the Cloud Run Admin API.
cards.explanation: A function created through the Cloud Run Admin API uses that API for management. The Cloud Functions API cannot modify these Admin API-created functions.
cards.misconception: The shared Cloud Run runtime makes the function creation APIs interchangeable for later updates.
cards.volatilityNote: Function management compatibility evolves as Google integrates the creation APIs.

cards.statement: Cloud Deploy can promote a release to a Cloud Run service target by creating a rollout.
cards.explanation: Cloud Deploy records a promotion as a new rollout associated with the existing release and destination target. The rollout tracks deployment of that release to the target.

cards.statement: Kubernetes Engine Cluster Viewer authorizes developers to inspect application Pods through the GKE Kubernetes API.
cards.explanation: Kubernetes Engine Cluster Viewer supplies cluster access information. A developer still needs IAM or Kubernetes RBAC authorization for workload actions inside the cluster.
cards.misconception: The Cluster Viewer role also grants permission to read workload objects through the Kubernetes API.

cards.statement: GKE Ingress copies later readiness probe edits into an already inferred load balancer health check.
cards.explanation: GKE Ingress infers health check parameters when it creates the load balancer. Later readiness probe changes leave that existing health check unchanged.
cards.misconception: A health check inferred from a readiness probe remains synchronized with later probe edits.

source.title: About GKE Ingress routing and security

cards.statement: GKE's built-in Artifact Registry pulls use the Pod's Workload Identity Federation for GKE identity.
cards.explanation: GKE uses the node pool's configured IAM service account to pull container images, including when Workload Identity Federation for GKE is enabled.
cards.misconception: A Pod's runtime federation identity supplies GKE's native credentials for pulling its image.

source.title: About Workload Identity Federation for GKE

cards.statement: GKE Image streaming can slow startup when an initializer reads many files from its container image.
cards.explanation: Image streaming serves image files through remote reads while initialization runs. Reading many files at startup can add enough latency to increase the application's initialization time.

source.title: Use Image streaming to pull container images

cards.statement: A GKE horizontal Pod autoscaler scales a message consumer using a configured Pub/Sub backlog metric.
cards.explanation: A Pub/Sub backlog metric gives a GKE autoscaler an external measure of demand. The configured queue threshold guides changes to the consumer's replica count.

cards.statement: The third-party Prometheus Adapter scopes Managed Service for Prometheus queries to the HPA's namespace.
cards.explanation: Prometheus Adapter queries are global in scope, so identically named metrics from other namespaces feed the HPA. Add namespace or cluster filters to the PromQL query.
cards.misconception: The Prometheus Adapter automatically restricts metric queries to the namespace containing the HPA.

cards.statement: GKE bounds the protection an application's PodDisruptionBudget provides during surge upgrades.
cards.explanation: During surge upgrades, GKE respects a workload's PodDisruptionBudget for a bounded drain period. It then forces remaining Pods off the node so the upgrade proceeds.

cards.statement: By default, Cloud Deploy runs a GKE target's verification containers in its execution environment, outside the cluster.
cards.explanation: Verification runs in the Cloud Deploy execution environment unless skaffold.yaml sets executionMode.kubernetesCluster on the verify containers, an option for GKE targets only.

cards.statement: A Firestore server SDK transaction callback that sends an email can send it twice for one commit.
cards.explanation: Server client libraries rerun the whole transaction callback after contention, while Firestore's atomic commit covers only database writes. Return data from the callback and send email after it succeeds.

cards.statement: Firestore Standard edition server transactions support reading a document after queuing a write.
cards.explanation: Firestore transaction code reads documents before queuing writes. Move dependent reads ahead of the transaction's set, update, or delete operations.
cards.misconception: Firestore transaction reads can follow writes in the same callback.

cards.statement: A Firestore web SDK transaction checks document versions at commit rather than locking the documents it reads.
cards.explanation: Mobile and web SDKs emulate optimistic concurrency with write preconditions on document versions, so they behave optimistically even when the database concurrency mode is PESSIMISTIC.

cards.statement: Cloud SQL Auth Proxy maintains a pool of PostgreSQL application connections for reuse across requests.
cards.explanation: Cloud SQL Auth Proxy provides authorized connectivity. Configure a separate pool when the application needs to reuse PostgreSQL connections.
cards.misconception: Cloud SQL Auth Proxy maintains an application connection pool.

source.title: About the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy

cards.statement: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL apps need their own retry logic for a transaction cut off by a lost connection.
cards.explanation: Pools and backoff help when opening a connection, but the application must retry a transaction interrupted mid-way from its beginning; a well-configured pool still surfaces lost connections.

cards.statement: A Cloud Storage resumable uploader treats locally sent bytes as proof of persisted progress after interruption.
cards.explanation: Check the resumable session's status. The response's Range header identifies persisted bytes, so continue after its upper offset; an absent Range means start at the beginning.
cards.misconception: A resumable upload's local sent-byte count proves how much Cloud Storage persisted.

cards.statement: Supported Pub/Sub client libraries expose acknowledgment results for an exactly-once pull subscription.
cards.explanation: Inspect a supported client's acknowledgment response to learn whether Pub/Sub accepted the request.

cards.statement: A Pub/Sub pull subscriber with exactly-once delivery can reuse the first acknowledgment ID after redelivery.
cards.explanation: A valid redelivery creates a new acknowledgment ID. Pub/Sub accepts the latest ID; an older delivery's ID fails.
cards.misconception: The first acknowledgment ID remains valid after Pub/Sub redelivers a message.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub exactly-once pull delivery deduplicates repeated publishes of the same application event.
cards.explanation: Publisher retries can create separate messages for the same event. Pub/Sub exactly-once delivery leaves those publish-side duplicates possible.
cards.misconception: Exactly-once delivery removes duplicates created by publishing the same event again.

cards.statement: Service Usage returns an operation for services.enable that an app checks for successful completion.
cards.explanation: The returned long-running operation lets a Service Usage caller track completion of services.enable. Check for successful completion before assuming the requested API is ready.

cards.statement: Google APIs Explorer can send object-delete API requests to a temporary copy of the specified resource.
cards.explanation: Google APIs Explorer sends requests to actual APIs and resource data. A create, modify, or delete call can change the real resources selected in the request.
cards.misconception: The API documentation's interactive explorer uses isolated copies of resources for mutations.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage JSON API object listings can include nextPageToken on a page shorter than maxResults.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage can return fewer object-list entries than requested while more pages remain. Continue using nextPageToken; counting a page's entries is insufficient to detect the end.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage JSON API batches can enforce call dependencies by executing request parts in submitted order.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage may execute batch requests in a different order from their submitted parts. Send a dependent call separately after the prerequisite call completes.
cards.misconception: The sequence of request parts within a batch establishes execution dependencies.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage JSON API preserves parent objects when a partial response selects a nested metadata field.
cards.explanation: A Cloud Storage JSON API fields selector returns the selected nested value inside its enclosing objects. Application code still reads the original JSON hierarchy, with unselected sibling fields omitted.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage sets a download's Cache-Control response header from the caller's Cache-Control request header.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage derives a download's Cache-Control response header from the object's stored metadata. It ignores the caller's Cache-Control request header when setting that response value.
cards.misconception: The download request's caching header overrides Cloud Storage's stored object caching metadata.

cards.statement: A client can safely retry a Cloud Storage JSON API upload after transient errors using the same ifGenerationMatch.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage classifies object inserts with a generation-match precondition as conditionally idempotent. Retry a transient failure using the same precondition to preserve that protection.

cards.statement: A Cloud Storage client fixes an HTTP 412 generation mismatch by retrying the request with the same precondition.
cards.explanation: A 412 means the object no longer matches the precondition. Request its current metadata, decide whether the change still applies, then send a new request with the current generation.
cards.misconception: A precondition mismatch is a transient failure resolved by resending the same stale condition.

cards.statement: Bigtable preserves the row's pre-request state when a write returns DEADLINE_EXCEEDED.
cards.explanation: Bigtable can return DEADLINE_EXCEEDED after a state-changing request has succeeded. A delayed response can outlive the deadline, so the error alone leaves the write's outcome uncertain.
cards.misconception: A deadline error proves that a Bigtable write had no effect on the stored row.

cards.statement: Cloud Logging promotes a Cloud Run service's stdout JSON severity field to the log entry's severity.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run's integrated logging moves the JSON severity property into LogEntry.severity. Severity filters then operate on that field rather than a value buried in jsonPayload.

source.title: Logging and viewing logs in Cloud Run

cards.statement: Cloud Run services associate plain-text container logs with the corresponding request log by default.
cards.explanation: Plain container logs need trace correlation to nest under a Cloud Run request log. Use the documented logging library behavior or a structured logging.googleapis.com/trace field.
cards.misconception: Cloud Run's collection of container logs also links plain-text messages to their HTTP request logs.

source.title: Logging and viewing logs in Cloud Run

cards.statement: Cloud Run's platform-generated spans measure individual database calls made by an HTTP handler.
cards.explanation: Cloud Run supplies request-level tracing. Application instrumentation adds spans that measure internal work such as a database call within the handler.
cards.misconception: Cloud Run's platform tracing supplies detailed spans for internal application operations.

cards.statement: An OpenTelemetry application can export spans through the Telemetry API using an OTLP exporter.
cards.explanation: Configure an in-process OTLP exporter to send trace data to the Telemetry API. This documented export path sends application spans to the Google Cloud project.

cards.statement: A trace header's sampled flag takes precedence over downstream Google Cloud services' sampling limits.
cards.explanation: Google Cloud services treat the sampled flag as a hint. Downstream components make their own sampling decisions and apply their own rate limits.
cards.misconception: Setting the sampling flag overrides a downstream Google Cloud service's sampling policy.

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring automatically creates a new custom metric's descriptor from a timeSeries.create write.
cards.explanation: A first timeSeries.create write can define a custom metric's descriptor from its data. Cloud Monitoring infers properties such as labels and value type, using defaults for other metadata.

source.title: Create user-defined metrics with the API

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring timeSeries.create accepts older samples after newer points in the same time series.
cards.explanation: Cloud Monitoring requires a new point to be more recent than the existing points in its time series. Application writers need to preserve timestamp order when sending buffered samples.
cards.misconception: Cloud Monitoring accepts out-of-order writes and rearranges a time series by timestamp.

cards.statement: Error Reporting captures a Cloud Run JSON log's plain text message when its @type identifies ReportedErrorEvent.
cards.explanation: Set jsonPayload.@type to type.googleapis.com/google.devtools.clouderrorreporting.v1beta1.ReportedErrorEvent. Error Reporting then captures the accompanying text message as an error event.

source.title: Format a log entry to report error events

cards.statement: Cloud Profiler's Node.js agent collects CPU-time profiles for diagnosing slow production handlers.
cards.explanation: Cloud Profiler offers heap and wall-time profiles for Node.js, not CPU time. A wall-time profile also counts time a handler spends waiting.
cards.misconception: The Cloud Profiler Node.js agent offers the same CPU-time profile type as its Go or Java agents.
